rows.evidence: Q1: Materials and methods / Results <U+2013> three-year (2019<U+2013>2021) replicated greenhouse field trial at Yangling, Shaanxi, with three treatments (CK, FP conventional drip fertigation, IF intelligent sensor-controlled drip fertigation); own measurements of irrigation volumes, yield, IWUE, nutrient uptake, root morphology and fruit quality.
rows.notes: The study is a primary experiment, but every treatment (CK, FP and IF) is irrigated by drip; there is no non-drip comparator. What the study actually shows is that sensor-controlled (intelligent) scheduling of drip fertigation saved 29<U+2013>37% irrigation water and raised IWUE by 61<U+2013>73% relative to farmers' conventional drip fertigation, while cutting N, P2O5 and K2O rates by 46<U+2013>72% without yield or quality loss (Fig. 2, Table 6). Like a mulch-versus-no-mulch trial under drip, this is evidence about the differentiating factor (automatic soil-moisture-based control and stage-specific fertilizer splitting), not about drip fertigation as such delivering water conservation or efficient water/fertilizer use. The passage's broad claim about drip fertigation's advantages is therefore not directly supported by the study's own comparison, so Q2 is 'no' and Q3<U+2013>Q9 follow. Single site, single crop, plot scale (28 m2 plots); water saving reported as a percentage per year without dispersion measures; no explicit limitations of the result stated beyond noting high system cost as an adoption barrier.

notes: Full text appears complete (abstract absent, tables/figures referenced but not reproduced). The study compares intelligent versus conventional drip fertigation; both arms use drip, so it cannot isolate the effect of drip fertigation itself.
